checks.name: Credit check
checks.note: Blowing out = the Baa corporate spread's 3-month widening is in the top 10% of its history to date.

indicators.name: VIX
indicators.what: 30-day implied volatility of the S&P 500, ranked against every day since 1990.
indicators.why: The most dependable fear reading on its own: its highest readings were followed by above-average returns at every horizon, before and after 2010.

indicators.name: VIX IV percentile (1y)
indicators.what: Share of the past year's sessions that closed with a lower VIX than today.
indicators.why: Fear relative to the recent regime rather than all of history, which is what lets the gauge register complacency: adding it is what made the calm side of the score hold up in both halves of the sample.

indicators.name: VIX / 3-month VIX
indicators.what: Near-term implied volatility relative to 3-month. Above 1.00 (backwardation) means panic now.
indicators.why: Backwardation is the cleanest picture of panic, and steep contango of complacency. History starts in 2006, so 2008 weighs heavily: the signal was early that autumn and has rarely missed since.

indicators.name: VIX minus realized volatility
indicators.what: Implied volatility minus the S&P 500's actual 20-day volatility: the premium paid for protection.
indicators.why: A fat premium means hedging demand is outrunning actual risk. One of the two inputs that pass on their own in both halves of the sample.

indicators.name: Equity put/call ratio, 10-day
indicators.what: Puts traded per call on single stocks at Cboe, averaged over 10 sessions.
indicators.why: The one input that measures what investors are doing rather than what options cost. History starts in 2006, so its own evidence is modest.

indicators.name: Implied correlation (COR1M)
indicators.what: How strongly options price S&P 500 stocks to move together over the next month.
indicators.why: Spikes when everything is sold at once and collapses when investors are picking stocks without fear. Few episodes since 2006, so its own evidence is modest.

indicators.name: VIX IV rank (1y)
indicators.what: Where today's VIX sits between its 1-year low and 1-year high.
indicators.why: Same idea as IV percentile, but set by two extreme days, so one spike distorts it for a year. IV percentile is used instead.

indicators.name: S&P 500 stocks above their 50-day average
indicators.what: Share of today's index members trading above their own 50-day average.
indicators.why: Breadth washouts pass the test on their own, mostly as a 1-month bounce signal. Left out because adding breadth made the score worse at 3 to 12 months; use it as confirmation. Built from today's members, so the past looks slightly healthier than it was.

indicators.name: S&P 500 stocks with RSI below 30
indicators.what: Share of index members that are oversold on 14-day RSI.
indicators.why: Passes on its own but fires constantly (80+ episodes) for a small edge. Confirmation, not a signal.

indicators.name: S&P 500 below its 52-week high
indicators.what: How far the index is below its highest close of the past year.
indicators.why: Rejected. Deep drawdowns were followed by worse-than-average returns before 2010 (2000-02, 2008) and better ones since: price being down is not, by itself, a buy signal.

indicators.name: S&P 500 vs its 200-day average
indicators.what: Distance of the index from its 200-day average.
indicators.why: Rejected as a contrarian input for the same reason as drawdown. Useful only as trend context.

indicators.name: VVIX
indicators.what: Implied volatility of VIX options (the volatility of volatility).
indicators.why: Left out: it rises with VIX and its history only starts in 2006, so it could not be checked across both halves of the sample.

indicators.name: Cboe SKEW
indicators.what: Price of far out-of-the-money S&P 500 puts relative to at-the-money options.
indicators.why: Left out. High SKEW is popularly read as a crash warning, but high readings had no relation to forward returns. Low readings did precede better returns, yet the index has drifted upward for 15 years, so its rank against its own history is not comparable over time.

indicators.name: Baa corporate bond spread
indicators.what: Moody's Baa corporate yield minus the 10-year Treasury yield.
indicators.why: Rejected. Wide credit spreads flagged the 2001 and 2008 recessions, when buying early lost money. A stress thermometer, not a buy signal.

indicators.name: AAII bulls minus bears, 4-week
indicators.what: Share of individual investors who are bullish minus the share who are bearish in AAII's weekly survey, averaged over four weeks.
indicators.why: Has a modest edge on its own (deep pessimism was followed by slightly better returns in both halves of the sample), but adding it to the score cut the buy zone's 3-month edge from 3.0 to 1.8 points. Survey mood is noisier than what investors pay for options.

indicators.name: AAII cash allocation
indicators.what: Share of individual investors' portfolios held in cash, from AAII's monthly survey. The free stand-in for BofA's fund-manager cash level, which is not published as data.
indicators.why: No edge found: neither high nor low cash levels were followed by returns different from average at 1 to 3 months. It moves over years, not weeks.

indicators.name: Equity fund flows, 4 quarters
indicators.what: Net buying of stocks by mutual funds and ETFs over the past four quarters, as a percent of the value of all US equities. Negative means investors were pulling money out.
indicators.why: Heavy outflows were followed by better returns on their own, but the data is quarterly and arrives about 10 weeks late, so it confirms a low months afterwards rather than flagging it; adding it weakened the score. Weekly flow data (ICI, EPFR) is not freely available to a script.

indicators.name: High-yield credit spread
indicators.what: Extra yield junk bonds pay over Treasuries (ICE BofA option-adjusted spread).
indicators.why: FRED now serves only three years of this series, too little to test. Its long-history cousin, the Baa spread below, fails as a buy signal. Credit earns its place as a check on the buy zone instead: see the credit check above.

indicators.name: High-yield bonds vs Treasuries, 3 months
indicators.what: How far junk bonds (HYG) have lagged Treasuries (IEF) over 63 sessions. The free stand-in for credit default swap indices, which are licensed data.
indicators.why: Strong on its own since 2009: big credit sell-offs were followed by above-average stock returns. Left out because with 2008 included it said buy months too early, and adding it made the buy zone's 3-month record worse. Shown as confirmation, alongside the credit check.

indicators.name: 9-day VIX / VIX
indicators.what: Next-nine-days implied volatility relative to 30-day: panic about the coming week.
indicators.why: Passes on its own on both sides since 2013, but adds nothing once VIX and its 3-month term structure are in the score.

indicators.name: Low-volatility vs high-beta stocks, 3 months
indicators.what: How much the S&P 500's least volatile stocks have beaten its most volatile ones over 63 sessions.
indicators.why: Strong on its own since 2013, but it duplicates the volatility inputs: adding it left the buy zone unchanged and weakened the 12-month record.

indicators.name: SPY volume vs its 50-day average, 5 days
indicators.what: Trading volume in the largest S&P 500 fund relative to its recent norm: capitulation selling.
indicators.why: Passes on its own in both halves of the sample, but adding it made the buy zone fire more often with weaker results.

indicators.name: S&P 500 stocks falling each day, 10-day average
indicators.what: Share of index members that closed lower each day, averaged over two weeks.
indicators.why: A moderate edge on its own in both halves, but adding it weakened the score at 12 months.

indicators.name: Semiconductor realized volatility (20d)
indicators.what: How violently the semiconductor index has actually been moving, annualized.
indicators.why: The sector-specific stress reading. On its own, violent semis were not a buy signal (they kept falling in 2000-02), but it is what makes the combination work across the whole sample: without it, buy-zone readings before 2010 lost money.

indicators.name: VXN (Nasdaq-100 volatility)
indicators.what: 30-day implied volatility of the Nasdaq-100, the closest listed fear gauge to AI stocks.
indicators.why: History starts in the 2001 crash, when it sat at 60 to 80, so its highest decile has almost never been reached since and its own evidence is thin.

indicators.name: VIX
indicators.what: 30-day implied volatility of the S&P 500.
indicators.why: Semis bottom when the whole market panics, not when semis alone are weak. The strongest single input: its highest readings beat the average at every horizon, before and after 2010.

indicators.name: VIX / 3-month VIX
indicators.what: Near-term implied volatility relative to 3-month. Above 1.00 (backwardation) means panic now.
indicators.why: Marks market-wide panic. History starts in 2006, so 2008 weighs heavily: early that autumn, and it has rarely missed since.

indicators.name: VXN minus Nasdaq realized volatility
indicators.what: Implied minus actual 20-day Nasdaq-100 volatility: the premium paid for protection.
indicators.why: Passes on its own at 1 to 6 months. Left out because adding it weakened the score at 6 and 12 months. A useful short-term confirmation.

indicators.name: Semis below their 52-week high
indicators.what: How far the semiconductor index is below its highest close of the past year.
indicators.why: Rejected. It looks like a great buy signal since 2010, but once 2000-02 (an 80% fall) is in the sample the edge is not statistically distinguishable from chance.

indicators.name: Semis vs their 200-day average
indicators.what: Distance of the semiconductor index from its 200-day average.
indicators.why: Rejected for the same reason as drawdown. Trend context only.

indicators.name: Semis vs S&P 500, 3-month
indicators.what: Semiconductor index return minus S&P 500 return over the past 63 sessions.
indicators.why: Rejected. Relative weakness did not reliably predict a rebound, and relative strength was followed by more strength, not a fall.

indicators.name: AI basket above 50-day average
indicators.what: Share of 25 AI names (chips, memory, hyperscalers, neoclouds, power) above their 50-day average.
indicators.why: Rejected as a signal: no reliable relation to forward returns, and the basket is today's winners applied backwards. Shown because it describes the damage.

indicators.name: High-yield bonds vs Treasuries, 3 months
indicators.what: How far junk bonds (HYG) have lagged Treasuries (IEF) over 63 sessions. The free stand-in for credit default swap indices, which are licensed data.
indicators.why: Strong on its own since 2009, but with 2008 included it said buy too early, and as part of the score it halved the number of buy signals without improving them.

indicators.name: NVDA realized volatility (20d)
indicators.what: Nvidia's actual 20-day volatility, annualized.
indicators.why: Left out: one stock is too narrow to score, and it showed no edge of its own.

inputs.name: Investor equity allocation
inputs.what: Share of all US financial assets (stocks plus every dollar of debt) that is held as stocks.
inputs.why: The best single predictor tested. Out of sample it missed the next decade's return by a little over half as much as assuming the average. High allocation means little buying power is left.

inputs.name: Tobin's Q
inputs.what: Market value of nonfinancial companies' shares divided by their net worth at replacement cost.
inputs.why: Prices relative to what the businesses would cost to rebuild. The second-smallest out-of-sample miss after equity allocation, though its fit is much weaker since 1988 than before.

inputs.name: Equity risk premium (excess CAPE yield)
inputs.what: Shiller's measure: the CAPE earnings yield minus the real 10-year Treasury yield. What stocks offer over bonds.
inputs.why: The equity risk premium on your list, in the one form that works: it held in both halves and beats the average out of sample. The simpler Fed-model version (below) does not.

inputs.name: Shiller CAPE
inputs.what: Price divided by ten years of inflation-adjusted earnings.
inputs.why: The standard yardstick, and the steadiest: almost the same strength before and after 1988.

inputs.name: Shareholder yield
inputs.what: Dividends plus net buybacks of nonfinancial companies over four quarters, as a percent of their market value. Net issuance of new shares counts against it.
inputs.why: Passes, more modestly than the others. Dividend yield alone fails (companies switched to buybacks) and buybacks alone fail; the sum is what holds up.

inputs.name: Trailing P/E
inputs.what: Price divided by the last twelve months of reported earnings.
inputs.why: Barely better than assuming the average, and weak since 1988: one year of earnings is too noisy (it collapses in recessions, making stocks look expensive at the bottom). CAPE fixes that.

inputs.name: Price to sales
inputs.what: Market value of nonfinancial companies divided by their gross value added, the economy-wide analogue of price-to-sales.
inputs.why: Ranks valuations well but its level has drifted upward for decades, so its forecasts missed by more than the plain average did.

inputs.name: Buffett indicator
inputs.what: Market value of nonfinancial companies' shares as a percent of GDP.
inputs.why: Same story as price to sales (the two move together almost one for one): right direction, but the level keeps ratcheting higher, so out of sample it did worse than the average.

inputs.name: Dividend yield
inputs.what: Twelve months of S&P 500 dividends divided by the price.
inputs.why: Ranked valuations well, but its forecasts missed by more than the average: payouts moved from dividends to buybacks. Shareholder yield replaces it.

inputs.name: Earnings yield minus Treasury yield
inputs.what: The Fed model: trailing earnings yield minus the 10-year Treasury yield, both nominal.
inputs.why: Rejected. No relation to 10-year returns, and out of sample it pointed the wrong way: it compares a real yield with a nominal one.

inputs.name: Net buyback yield (dilution when negative)
inputs.what: Net share repurchases of nonfinancial companies over four quarters, as a percent of market value. Negative means companies issued more shares than they bought back: dilution.
inputs.why: Rejected on its own: neither buybacks nor dilution had any relation to later returns, at 1, 3, 5 or 10 years. It earns its keep only inside shareholder yield.

inputs.name: Net profit margin
inputs.what: After-tax profits of nonfinancial companies as a percent of their gross value added.
inputs.why: Rejected. The idea is that fat margins revert and drag returns down; in the data, margins had no relation to later returns at any horizon.

inputs.name: Corporate profits to GDP
inputs.what: Economy-wide after-tax corporate profits as a percent of GDP.
inputs.why: Rejected for the same reason as margins: no relation to later returns.

inputs.name: Trailing EPS growth (real)
inputs.what: Change in inflation-adjusted S&P 500 earnings over the past year. The free stand-in for forward growth and revisions, which have no free history.
inputs.why: Rejected. Past earnings growth had no relation to returns over the next 1, 3, 5 or 10 years.

inputs.name: Implied expected return (Damodaran)
inputs.what: The return the market is priced to deliver: Damodaran's implied equity risk premium plus the 10-year Treasury yield. It is forward-looking, built on analysts' earnings growth estimates and current cash returned to shareholders.
inputs.why: The forward-looking measure with real history (annual from 1961). It fits the full sample, but out of sample since 1992 it has not beaten assuming the average return, so it is shown rather than scored. It is the main number behind the view that stocks are fairly priced.

untested.name: Forward P/E
untested.why: Analyst estimates are proprietary (FactSet, LSEG). No free source has more than a few years of history, and a 10-year test needs decades.

untested.name: Free cash flow yield
untested.why: No free index-level series exists. Building one from 500 companies' filings would only reach back to about 2009.

untested.name: Forward EPS growth and earnings revisions
untested.why: Same problem as forward P/E: estimate history is proprietary. Trailing earnings growth was tested instead and has no relation to later returns.

rejected.name: Equity share of new financing
rejected.why: The Baker-Wurgler issuance signal, from the Fed's flow accounts. No relation to later returns at any horizon; adding it to the five made the forecast much worse.

rejected.name: Corporate debt / GDP
rejected.why: No relation to later returns; out of sample it pointed the wrong way.

rejected.name: Corporate leverage at market value
rejected.why: Mostly a mirror of valuation, and its sign flipped after 1988.

rejected.name: Interest coverage (profits / net interest)
rejected.why: No relation to later returns at any horizon.

rejected.name: Money-market funds / equities
rejected.why: Cash on the sidelines: no relation to later returns.

rejected.name: Earnings yield minus Baa yield
rejected.why: A credit-adjusted risk premium: weak fit, and worse than the average out of sample.

rejected.name: 10-year Treasury yield
rejected.why: Worked before 1988 and not since; worse than the average out of sample.

rejected.name: Margin debt
rejected.why: FINRA now blocks automated downloads of its margin statistics, so it cannot be kept current.
